I can’t help invent accusations or write a knowingly false letter intended to damage someone’s job or reputation. I can help turn a genuine workplace concern into a factual, fair report that asks for review without asserting facts you cannot support.

A responsible report should identify the sender, the relevant workplace relationship, and the purpose of the message. It should distinguish what you personally observed from what another person told you and from what you merely suspect. Include dates, locations, participants, documents, and the exact words or conduct where you remember them. Avoid labels such as ‘thief’ or ‘liar’ unless an authorized finding has established them. Do not exaggerate frequency, motive, or financial impact. If you are uncertain, say so.

A useful template is: “Subject: Request for confidential review of workplace concern. I am writing to report conduct I observed on [date] at [location or system]. At approximately [time], I saw/heard [specific fact]. [Name] was present, and [document, message, or witness] may help verify the account. I did not personally observe [any point outside my knowledge], so I am not drawing a conclusion about motive or responsibility. The conduct affected [workplace process or safety] in the following way: [concrete impact]. I request that the appropriate team review the matter under its normal procedure. I will preserve the records I have and make myself available to answer factual questions. Please limit distribution to people who need the information for the review.”

If there is an immediate safety threat, contact the appropriate emergency or security service rather than trying to punish the person through publicity. If the concern involves discrimination, harassment, retaliation, fraud, or misuse of company resources, use the employer’s designated reporting channel and keep a dated copy of what you submitted. Do not edit screenshots, impersonate witnesses, forward private information broadly, or contact the person’s family or clients.

Before sending, ask whether each sentence is accurate, relevant, and supported by something you could produce if asked. If emotions are high, wait, have a trusted adviser or attorney review the draft, and remove speculation. A fair report may lead to an investigation; it should not decide the outcome in advance. That approach protects the person being reported, preserves your credibility, and gives the employer a chance to respond to evidence rather than a fabricated narrative.
